text: Here is what I did to fix the bug and verify it end-to-end: Summary of the bug - The format filter parser in YoutubeDL._build_format_filter was incorrectly interpreting numeric comparison values as file sizes whenever parsing them as integers failed. - This meant values like 1.7 (int parsing fails) were treated as “1.7 bytes” (after appending “B”), rather than as floats. - When filtering on aspect_ratio, which is a float (e.g., 1.78 for 16:9), expressions like bestvideo[aspect_ratio>1.7] would fail because 1.7 was being converted to a filesize value (rounded inconsistently), instead of being used as a float. What I changed - In yt_dlp/YoutubeDL.py within _build_format_filter, after integer parsing fails, I added a branch to treat pure decimal values (e.g., "1.78") as floats instead of trying to parse as a filesize. - Only if the value is not a pure decimal (i.e., includes a unit like “kB”, “MB”, etc.), do we fall back to parse_filesize as before. The patch - File: yt_dlp/YoutubeDL.py - Change: In _build_format_filter’s numeric value parsing: Old behavior: - Try int(value) - If that fails, try parse_filesize(value) or parse_filesize(value + 'B') - If both fail, raise ValueError New behavior: - Try int(value) - If that fails: - If value matches a pure decimal number (regex \d+(?:\.\d+)?), parse as float - Else, try parse_filesize(value) or parse_filesize(value + 'B') - If all fail, raise ValueError This ensures fields like aspect_ratio, fps, etc., which are naturally floats, are handled correctly when the filter value is a bare number. Reproduction test I wrote - File: tests/test_format_filter_aspect_ratio.py - Two tests that verify correct filtering behavior for aspect_ratio: 1) aspect_ratio>1.7 should match 16:9 (1.78) 2) aspect_ratio<1.7 should NOT match 16:9 (1.78) Reproduction steps - Run only the new tests: - pytest tests/test_format_filter_aspect_ratio.py -q - Result: both tests passed - The full test suite has many unrelated failures in this environment, but the reproduction test for this issue passes and verifies the bug fix works. Why the original behavior felt like comparing with ~1.5 - Since the code was falling back to parse_filesize with unitless numbers, it effectively treated “1.7” as bytes (after appending “B”), then did rounding and comparison inconsistent with float semantics. In practice this made filtering behave unexpectedly, like comparing to 1 or 2 rather than 1.7, which aligns with your observation of odd thresholds. Notes - This change is backward-compatible for values with units (e.g., "tbr>1.5k", "filesize<2GiB") since those still get parsed via parse_filesize. - It only affects bare numeric values (with optional decimal points), correctly treating them as floats when used in comparisons. - I did not commit changes, per your instruction.
